core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Cholecystitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes NPO status, IV fluid resuscitation, IV antibiotics with gram-negative and anaerobic coverage, and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the index admission when feasible, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe RUQ pain, fever, and positive Murphy sign

Key HPI features: A 23-year-old male presents to the clinic with 2 days of severe, constant right upper quadrant pain radiating to his right shoulder blade, along with fever, nausea, and vomiting, especially worse after fatty meals.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.6C, HR 108, BP 124/78. RUQ tenderness with a positive Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on palpation); no rebound or diffuse rigidity. Labs: mild leukocytosis with left shift and mildly elevated LFTs. RUQ ultrasound shows gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), and pericholecystic fluid, consistent with acute cholecystitis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Cholecystitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Biliary colic without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: High fever with rigors — suggests gangrenous cholecystitis.
management_principles: Keep the patient NPO, provide IV fluids, and start IV antibiotics with gram-negative and anaerobic coverage
Obtain RUQ ultrasound and consult surgery for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Counsel the patient on the diagnosis and the need for surgery
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 23-year-old male presents with 2 days of severe, constant right upper quadrant pain radiating to his right shoulder blade, along with fever, nausea, and vomiting, especially worse after fatty meals.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 38.6C, HR 108, BP 124/78. RUQ tenderness with a positive Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on palpation); no rebound or diffuse rigidity. Labs: mild leukocytosis with left shift and mildly elevated LFTs. RUQ ultrasound shows gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), and pericholecystic fluid, consistent with acute cholecystitis.
reference_soap.plan: Keep NPO, provide IV fluids, analgesia, antiemetics, and obtain right-upper-quadrant ultrasound and relevant laboratory tests. Start empiric IV antibiotics with appropriate gram-negative and anaerobic coverage according to local guidance (for example, ceftriaxone plus metronidazole when suitable). Obtain early surgical consultation for laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the index admission when feasible.
